subject: Is there functionality in RStan for sampling from linear inverse problems?

messages.author: 8bff2513f06ee467
messages.subject: Is there functionality in RStan for sampling from linear inverse problems?
parts:
Other names for this problem are "sampling from a convex polytope" or "sampling from the solution space of a linear programming problem". The mathematical definition is sampling uniformly from the set {x | Ax = b, x>0}, or sampling from the set of solutions of Ax = b, for some matrix A and vector b, where all the components of x are positive, assuming a bounded space.

I have implemented a hit-and-run sampler for the problem, it is located at https://github.com/davidkane9/kmatching. However, when running the Gelman-Rubin diagnostic on multiple chains, it becomes clear that we would need to run an impractical number of samples in order to converge to a stationary distribution. 

Have there ever been problems of the same nature solved by RStan, if so, what specific functions should I look at?

Attached is a problem statement.

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Is there functionality in RStan for sampling from linear inverse problems?
parts:
Attachment was missing. Google might have eaten it, but I think PDFs should work.

As to your question, I'm not aware of this being done in Stan before. For a non-singular A, you could define x as a transformed parameter

x <- inverse(A) * b;

and rejecting the proposal if any element of x is negative. But putting a uniform prior on x would be a challenge. And your question seems to imply that A has short rank, so then it would be even more challenging.

Ben

messages.author: 8bff2513f06ee467
messages.subject: Re: Is there functionality in RStan for sampling from linear inverse problems?
parts: Yes, the number of rows of A is usually much less than the number of columns, giving the solution space (ncol(A)-nrow(A)) dimensions. A basic case would be the unit simplex, where A = [1,1,1] and b = 1 (and if x = [x,y,z] this is equivalent to the equation x+y+z = 1). There are ways to sample from that space that do not require a random walk (x = rexp(3); x = x/sum(x)), however this changes when you add rows of A, which is equivalent to slicing the solution space by a plane.

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Is there functionality in RStan for sampling from linear inverse problems?
parts:
For the special case of the simplex, Stan does have that. But in general, this seems like a hard problem for Stan. You could get a basis for the nullspace of A via the SVD and construct a linear function of that. But I don't know how to make the solution uniformally distributed over the non-negative reals.

Ben

messages.author: 8bff2513f06ee467
messages.subject: Re: Is there functionality in RStan for sampling from linear inverse problems?
parts: That's pretty much what my package does. The problem is making sure you are still in the space, it is indeed a hard problem. You can either reflect at the boundaries, then the running time goes up exponentially with the length of x, or you can pick a random direction and sample uniformly from the line connecting you with a limit of this space (where some of the inequalities are sharp). The second method is much faster, O(1) samples, but it gets stuck in corners, apparently. I think I'm going to try to do some parallel stuff.

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Is there functionality in RStan for sampling from linear inverse problems?
parts:
From a statistical perspective, perfect knowledge of the variables b is a bit presumptuous.  A more robust model allows measurement noise,

b ~ normal(A * x, sigma);

If A is known, then x and sigma can easily be inferred in Stan.  Positivity constrains on both are easily included in their definitions,

real<lower=0> x;
real<lower=0> sigma;

Additional constraints on x, such as a known sum, can be incorporated in the prior (for example, making the x a simplex and using a Dirichlet prior).

It's also straightforward to generalize when A is not known exactly by making it a parameter rather than data (I had great success in problems like this where A is a transfer matrix: model each column of A as a simplex with a Dirichlet prior and use any existing data to build a posterior for the columns that gets used as a prior for the joint inference).

parts:
Hi Michael,

As others have pointed out, Stan can't quite do exactly what you're asking (handle hard constraints on parameters) but it is able to do something close (as Michael B has described) by treating the (linear) constraints as soft.  If you're willing to implement your own HMC/NUTS like sampler you may want to take a look at:

http://www.cs.toronto.edu/~mbrubake/projects/cmcmc/

Cheers,
Marcus
